Some will be temporarily driven from their natural habitat. This temporary displacement is not expected to cause severe effects unless it occurs during a critical period of the life cycle of the particular animal. Certain animals will not be able to accommodate the opening of their habitat to ORV traffic and accompanying human activities. There would, accordingly, be displacement and movement of some creatures with subsequent disruption in established natural communities as these displaced animals attempt to fit in niches which, for all intents and purposes, are already filled.
ORV use would have significant adverse effects in many key wildlife areas within the lands administered by the Department. These areas include breeding, drumming, and spawning grounds, nesting and calving areas, winter range or feeding grounds, migratory routes and resting sites, and habitat for rare and endangered species. Where it is recognized that ORV use can have significant adverse effects upon fish and wildlife, such use will be prohibited.
On the other hand, ORV use permits access to wildlife areas where management practices can be instituted to control over-populous game and to prevent deterioration of habitat. In addition, on those public lands utilized for grazing, domestic animals in need of assistance can be more frequently and quickly discovered and their needs more readily met. Opening of public lands to ORV use would allow more fire-spotters and fire-fighters to remote areas resulting in earlier detection and control of fires with an attendant saving of animal and plant lives. Conversely, improper manufacture, maintenance, or operation of ORV can lead to an increased incidence of such fires.
C) Human Impacts:
The acquisition and use of ORV have increased dramatically in recent years with resultant economic impact on the United States and more particularly, in many towns and communities experiencing widespread ORV use. A 1971 study on off-road recreation vehicles by a Department of the Interior Task Force indicates that vehicle sales have created an economic boost to the general market. In 1971, the projected sales of motorcycles totaled $900 million, while projected snowmobile sales totaled $376 million.
Rural economies have felt significant increases due to snowmobile use in winter. Many small resort communities which were once dependent upon summer recreation now have business establishments which are open year long due to the winter use of snowmobiles. On a regional scale, Upper Great Lakes Regional Commission reported snowmobiling was worth $212,180,000 to the States of Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Michigan in 1970-71. The economic gains cited, while representative of ORV sales and operations, in no way reflect a total quantification of ORV economic impact; i.e., economic losses obviously occur in ORV accidents, and impacts may occur on certain crops, vegetation, soils, and other plant and animal ecosystems as a result of ORV use.
